abstract:
Hippocampal mossy fiber synapses act as powerful teacher synapses in CA3 memory networks, yet how their detonation properties are regulated remains unclear. Combining presynaptic and paired recordings, electron and expansion microscopy, and optogenetic stimulation in mouse hippocampal slices, we show that both exogenously applied baclofen and {gamma}-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synaptically released from inhibitory interneurons control transmission and plasticity at hippocampal mossy fiber synapses via presynaptic GABAB receptors. Presynaptic inhibition markedly changes the computational properties of the synapse, switching it from a detonation into a subdetonation mode. Powerful modulation is enabled by a combination of effects on release probability, mediated by the suppression of presynaptic Ca2+ inflow, and on the readily releasable vesicle pool, associated with a reduced number and increased dispersion of docked synaptic vesicles at the ultrastructural level. Synaptically released GABA reverses established post-tetanic potentiation, suggesting interference with vesicle storage mechanisms potentially underlying short-term memory ("vesicle pool engram"). Our results reveal a previously unrecognized inhibitory-excitatory interaction at a central excitatory synapse, in which presynaptic inhibition both sets the computational properties of transmission and limits the persistence of vesicle pool engrams. (181 words)
